title: Chapter 16 — That Excessive Care Of Worldly Welfare May Impair That Welfare
paragraphs: The improvement of the soul and the betterment of what belongs to the body are more closely tied together than people commonly suppose. Man may set the two apart and consider each in turn, but he cannot separate them entirely without finally losing sight of both. The beasts have the same senses we have and very nearly the same appetites. We have no sensual passions that our species does not share with them, or that cannot be found, at least in germ, in a dog as well as in a man. Why is it, then, that animals can provide only for their first and lowest wants, while we can vary our enjoyments without limit and increase them endlessly?

We are superior to the beasts in this: we use our souls to find the material benefits to which they are led only by instinct. In man, the angel teaches the brute the art of satisfying its desires. Because man can rise above the things of the body, and can even hold life in contempt — of which the beasts have not the least notion — he is able to multiply those same bodily things to a degree that lower creatures cannot conceive either. Whatever lifts, enlarges, and expands the soul makes it better able to succeed even in undertakings that do not concern it. Whatever, on the other hand, saps or lowers it weakens it for every purpose, the greatest as well as the least, and threatens to make it almost equally powerless for both. The soul must therefore remain great and strong, if only so that it can devote that strength and greatness from time to time to the service of the body. If men were ever to content themselves with material objects, they would probably lose by degrees the art of producing them, and in the end they would enjoy them like the brutes, without discernment and without improvement.
